title: Susceptibilities for Neural Networks Learning from Physical Data
claim: Sensitivity to a data-distribution parameter is large and structured early in training, then decays to zero, indicating calibration.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, shared chi axis, colorbars encode h and training step
description: Two line-plot panels share the y-axis quantity χ(h). Panel (a) plots χ(h) against training step on a log x-axis, with one line per value of h and shaded confidence bands. A viridis colorbar for h runs from purple at 0.35 to yellow at 0.60. Yellow and green curves start strongly positive, around +500 and +250. Purple and blue curves start strongly negative, around −450 and −250. All curves are noisy between 10^2 and 10^3 steps and then converge to zero by about 10^4 to 10^5 steps. Panel (b) plots χ(h) against h from 0.35 to 0.60, with error bars. Each line is a snapshot at one training step, colored by a plasma colorbar from dark blue at 10^3 to yellow at 10^5. Early curves are steep and cross zero near h=0.475. Later curves flatten to zero.
caption: The susceptibility χ(h) shows how the percolation model described in Section 4.1 becomes calibrated over all values of h in the training distribution (9); contrast this with χcrit.(h) in Figure 2 which shows the difficulty of learning percolation at different values of h. (a) χ(h) over training for various values of h. (b) χ(h) plotted as a function of h at various points over training. Observe that χ(h) is roughly symmetric about h ≈0.475 — mean value of h in the training distribution — at each point in training, and that χ(h) decays to zero over training for all h ∈[0.35, 0.6].
abstract: Neural networks that are trained on data arising from a physical system must somehow learn regularities induced by the underlying physical laws. In this setting, concepts from statistical physics provide powerful tools for analysing how physical laws influence the learning process. In this paper we explain how susceptibilities --- which measure the response of a neural network to perturbations of a parameter of the data distribution --- can be applied when learning from physical data. We show that such susceptibilities can identify the conditions under which specific input features are most informative for learning, guiding data selection, a prediction we validate experimentally. For distributions lacking a natural parameter, we propose introducing one via a physically meaningful scalar function of the physical state, and demonstrate that susceptibilities track the emergence of specific capabilities (such as collision detection) during training.
